1.1 Installing and Loading R Packages
Three packages are used in this exercise. sf handles the geospatial data, tmap draws the thematic maps, and tidyverse covers importing and wrangling.

title: Hands-on Exercise 1
text:
2.1 Importing Geospatial Data

2.1.1 Polygon feature data
data.gov.sg has retired the shapefile and KML versions of this layer, so the geojson is what is available. For geojson st_read() takes a single path rather than the dsn and layer pair the shapefile version needs.

mpsz <- st_read("data/geospatial/MasterPlan2014SubzoneBoundaryNoSea.geojson")

Reading layer `MP14_SUBZONE_NO_SEA_PL' from data source 
  `/Users/czxtom/Documents/Programming/GAA/ISSS626-GAA/Hands-on_Ex/Hands-on_Ex01/data/geospatial/MasterPlan2014SubzoneBoundaryNoSea.geojson' 
  using driver `GeoJSON'
Simple feature collection with 323 features and 13 fields
Geometry type: MULTIPOLYGON
Dimension:     XY
Bounding box:  xmin: 103.6057 ymin: 1.158699 xmax: 104.0885 ymax: 1.470775
Geodetic CRS:  WGS 84


323 features, 13 fields, multipolygon. Two things are different from the book. The layer comes in as WGS84, not SVY21. And the area and length fields are called SHAPE_1.AREA and SHAPE_1.LEN, not SHAPE_Area and SHAPE_Leng. Both of these bite me later.






NoteLearning diary



Small thing, but worth writing down. The 2019 file downloads as MasterPlan2019SubzoneBoundaryNoSeaGEOJSON.geojson, with GEOJSON in the middle of the name rather than just the extension. Nobody would guess that. Now I copy filenames out of ls instead of typing what I think they are called.




2.1.2 Polyline feature data

cyclingpath <- st_read(dsn = "data/geospatial",
                       layer = "CyclingPathGazette")

Reading layer `CyclingPathGazette' from data source 
  `/Users/czxtom/Documents/Programming/GAA/ISSS626-GAA/Hands-on_Ex/Hands-on_Ex01/data/geospatial' 
  using driver `ESRI Shapefile'
Simple feature collection with 4830 features and 7 fields
Geometry type: MULTILINESTRING
Dimension:     XY
Bounding box:  xmin: 11721.1 ymin: 27550.13 xmax: 42809.37 ymax: 49702.59
Projected CRS: SVY21


LTA gives this one as a shapefile, not geojson. So st_read() needs the dsn and layer pair instead of one path. Look at the CRS it reports too, this one is already in SVY21 while the data.gov.sg layers are not.






WarningIssue I hit



The zip unpacked into a folder called CyclingPath_Mar2026, so my files sat one level deeper than the code expected and st_read() could not find the layer. I moved the nine CyclingPathGazette.* files up into data/geospatial and it worked. Nothing clever, I just had not looked at where the unzip actually put them.




2.1.3 Point feature data

preschool <- st_read("data/geospatial/PreSchoolsLocation.geojson")

Reading layer `PreSchoolsLocation' from data source 
  `/Users/czxtom/Documents/Programming/GAA/ISSS626-GAA/Hands-on_Ex/Hands-on_Ex01/data/geospatial/PreSchoolsLocation.geojson' 
  using driver `GeoJSON'
Simple feature collection with 2290 features and 2 fields
Geometry type: POINT
Dimension:     XYZ
Bounding box:  xmin: 103.6878 ymin: 1.247759 xmax: 103.9897 ymax: 1.462134
z_range:       zmin: 0 zmax: 0
Geodetic CRS:  WGS 84


2290 point features, in WGS84.

names(preschool)

[1] "Name"        "Description" "geometry"   


Worth pausing on this. The preschool layer has no real attribute columns. Everything the file knows about each centre is packed into a single Description string as an HTML table, a quirk of how data.gov.sg exports these layers. Oddly the two Master Plan boundary layers do not have this problem, they come through with proper columns, so it is not consistent across data.gov.sg exports. Here it does not matter either way, because every use of preschool below relies only on the geometry.

The default plot of an sf object draws every attribute as its own small map.

plot(st_geometry(mpsz),
     col = "#EFE9DB", border = "grey65", lwd = 0.4,
     main = "Singapore planning subzones, Master Plan 2014")




Or a single named attribute.

     key.pos = NULL, border = "grey80", lwd = 0.3,
     main = "Subzones coloured by planning area")

title: Hands-on Exercise 1
text:
2.4 Working with Projection
Two layers can only be used together if they share a coordinate system, so this step is not optional.

2.4.1 Checking what we actually have

st_crs(mpsz)

Coordinate Reference System:
  User input: WGS 84 
  wkt:
GEOGCRS["WGS 84",
    DATUM["World Geodetic System 1984",
        ELLIPSOID["WGS 84",6378137,298.257223563,
            LENGTHUNIT["metre",1]]],
    PRIMEM["Greenwich",0,
        ANGLEUNIT["degree",0.0174532925199433]],
    CS[ellipsoidal,2],
        AXIS["geodetic latitude (Lat)",north,
            ORDER[1],
            ANGLEUNIT["degree",0.0174532925199433]],
        AXIS["geodetic longitude (Lon)",east,
            ORDER[2],
            ANGLEUNIT["degree",0.0174532925199433]],
    ID["EPSG",4326]]


Here my file and the book part ways, so I had to stop and think about it.
The book reads a shapefile that really is in SVY21 but has the wrong EPSG code attached. The coordinates are fine, only the label is wrong, so it fixes the label with st_set_crs(3414).
Mine is a different problem. It says WGS84 and it means it. The bounding box runs 103.6 to 104.0 across and 1.15 to 1.47 up, and those are degrees. SVY21 would give me metres in the tens of thousands.
So if I copied st_set_crs(3414) I would be sticking an SVY21 label on degree values without changing the numbers underneath. st_transform() is the one that actually converts them.






NoteLearning diary



This is the one that would have got me. Nothing errors either way. The map still draws, the code still runs, and every area and buffer after it is quietly wrong.
What saved me was reading the bounding box instead of skipping past it. Degrees look like 103.8. Metres look like 28,000. Once I noticed that, the rest was obvious.
The rule I am taking from this. st_set_crs fixes a wrong label. st_transform changes the actual coordinates. Ask which one is broken before picking.



mpsz3414 <- st_transform(mpsz, crs = 3414)


st_crs(mpsz3414)$epsg

[1] 3414



st_bbox(mpsz3414)

     xmin      ymin      xmax      ymax 
 2667.538 15748.721 56396.440 50256.334 


The bounding box is now in metres, in the tens of thousands. That is my quick check that the transform actually did something rather than just changing the label.


2.4.2 Transforming preschool to svy21
Same situation, same tool.

preschool3414 <- st_transform(preschool, crs = 3414)


st_geometry(preschool3414)

Geometry set for 2290 features 
Geometry type: POINT
Dimension:     XYZ
Bounding box:  xmin: 11810.03 ymin: 25596.33 xmax: 45404.24 ymax: 49300.88
z_range:       zmin: 0 zmax: 0
Projected CRS: SVY21 / Singapore TM
First 5 geometries:


Values well outside the 0 to 360 range of decimal degrees, so this one worked too.


2.4.3 Overlaying the two layers
Before the transform, the preschool points would not have landed on the subzone map at all. Now they do.

The PlotThe Code














plot(st_geometry(mpsz3414),
     col = "#F7F4EC", border = "grey72", lwd = 0.4,
     main = "2,290 pre-schools over the subzone boundaries")
plot(st_geometry(preschool3414), add = TRUE,
     pch = 21, cex = 0.42, bg = "#0072B2AA", col = "#00548A", lwd = 0.3)

2.5.2 Creating a simple feature data frame

listings_sf <- st_as_sf(listings,
                        coords = c("longitude", "latitude"),
                        crs = 4326) %>%
  st_transform(crs = 3414)

Three things about the arguments. coords wants x first then y, so longitude comes before latitude. crs = 4326 is WGS84, the system the raw coordinates are in. The piped st_transform() then moves it to 3414 to match everything else.

     col = "#F7F4EC", border = "grey72", lwd = 0.4,

title: Hands-on Exercise 1
text:
2.6 Geoprocessing with sf

2.6.1 Use case 1, land acquisition analysis
The scenario is that the authority wants to widen the existing cycling paths and needs 5 metres of reserved land on either side. The task is to work out how much land that comes to.
dist = 5 in st_buffer() means five units of whatever coordinate system the layer is in. On a WGS84 layer that would be five degrees, a buffer some 550 km wide, and it would run without error and give a meaningless answer.
The cycling path is the one layer here that already arrived in SVY21, so this transform changes nothing. I have kept it anyway rather than relying on LTA continuing to ship it that way. It costs nothing and it makes the assumption explicit.

cyclingpath3414 <- st_transform(cyclingpath, crs = 3414)
st_crs(cyclingpath3414)$epsg

[1] 3414


Now st_buffer() builds buffers that really are 5 metres.

buffer_cycling <- st_buffer(cyclingpath3414, dist = 5, nQuadSegs = 30)

Then the area of each buffer.

buffer_cycling <- buffer_cycling %>%
  mutate(AREA = st_area(geometry))

And the total.

sum(buffer_cycling$AREA)

3687875 [m^2]


To see what this looks like on the ground, we can clip the buffers to a single subzone. Tampines West here.

mpsz_selected <- mpsz3414 %>%
  filter(SUBZONE_N == "TAMPINES WEST")

buffer_cycling_selected <- st_intersection(buffer_cycling, mpsz_selected)


The PlotThe Code














plot(st_geometry(mpsz_selected),
     col = "#F7F4EC", border = "grey55", lwd = 0.8,
     main = "Five metre reserve along cycling paths, Tampines West")
plot(st_geometry(buffer_cycling_selected), add = TRUE,
     col = "#D55E00", border = NA)






2.6.2 Use case 2, counting pre-schools by planning subzone
The scenario is that the authority needs a pre-school count for every planning subzone to feed into forward planning.
st_intersects() returns, for each subzone, the list of preschools falling inside it. Wrapping that in lengths() turns the lists into counts in one step.

mpsz3414$`PreSch Count` <- lengths(st_intersects(mpsz3414, preschool3414))

This is st_intersects(), not st_intersection().






NoteLearning diary



These two are one letter apart and do different jobs, so this is worth saying out loud before typing either. st_intersects() answers which things overlap and gives you a list. st_intersection() cuts the shapes and gives you the overlapping pieces back. Only the first one is any use for counting.



summary(mpsz3414$`PreSch Count`)

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
   0.00    0.00    4.00    7.09   10.00   72.00 


The median subzone has only a handful of pre-schools while the maximum is far higher, so the distribution is heavily skewed.

top_n(mpsz3414, 1, `PreSch Count`)

Simple feature collection with 1 feature and 14 fields
Geometry type: MULTIPOLYGON
Dimension:     XY
Bounding box:  xmin: 39655.33 ymin: 35966 xmax: 42940.57 ymax: 38622.37
Projected CRS: SVY21 / Singapore TM
  OBJECTID_1 SUBZONE_NO     SUBZONE_N SUBZONE_C CA_IND PLN_AREA_N PLN_AREA_C
1        204          2 TAMPINES EAST    TMSZ02      N   TAMPINES         TM
     REGION_N REGION_C          INC_CRC     FMEL_UPD_D SHAPE_1.AREA SHAPE_1.LEN
1 EAST REGION       ER 21658EAAF84F4D8D 20160511160621      4339824    10180.62
                        geometry PreSch Count
1 MULTIPOLYGON (((42196.76 38...           72


Counts on their own are misleading because subzones differ a lot in size, so we convert to a density per square kilometre.

mpsz3414$Area <- mpsz3414 %>%
  st_area()

mpsz3414 <- mpsz3414 %>%
  mutate(`PreSch Density` = `PreSch Count` / Area * 1000000)



2.6.3 Exploratory data analysis
The base R histogram is quick but hard to customise.

The PlotThe Code














dens <- as.numeric(mpsz3414$`PreSch Density`)

hist(dens,
     breaks = 20, col = "#CFE3F0", border = "white",
     main = "Pre-school density is heavily skewed",
     xlab = "Pre-schools per square kilometre",
     ylab = "Number of subzones")
abline(v = median(dens, na.rm = TRUE), col = "#D55E00", lwd = 2, lty = 2)
legend("topright", bty = "n", col = "#D55E00", lwd = 2, lty = 2,
       legend = sprintf("median %.1f", median(dens, na.rm = TRUE)))




ggplot2 gives a far more presentable version, with room for a proper title and axis labels.

The PlotThe Code














ggplot(data = mpsz3414,
       aes(x = as.numeric(`PreSch Density`))) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20,
                 color = "black",
                 fill = "light blue") +
  labs(title = "Are pre-schools evenly distributed in Singapore?",
       subtitle = "Most subzones have very few pre-schools, while a small number have a great many",
       x = "Pre-school density (per km sq)",
       y = "Frequency")




Same story as the summary. Over a hundred subzones are in the lowest bin and the count drops off fast after that, with a few stragglers past 30 per square kilometre.
A scatterplot of count against density shows how the two relate.

The PlotThe Code














ggplot(data = mpsz3414,
       aes(y = `PreSch Count`,
           x = as.numeric(`PreSch Density`))) +
  geom_point(color = "black") +
  xlim(0, 40) +
  ylim(0, 40) +
  labs(x = "Pre-school density (per km sq)",
       y = "Pre-school count")




Count and density do rise together, but the spread is wide. Two subzones with the same density can be twenty pre-schools apart. The points on the far right, around 35 per square kilometre, only have a few pre-schools each because those subzones are small.


Watch the axis limits. xlim and ylim stop at 40 here. Anything past that is dropped from the plot without a warning, so an outlier just vanishes instead of showing up.
One thing to watch. xlim and ylim cut the axes at 40, so any point past that is dropped from the plot instead of showing up as an outlier. The chart looks tidier than the data actually is.

title: Hands-on Exercise 1
text:
3.1 Importing the Data
This half uses two different datasets, the Master Plan 2019 subzone boundaries and the 2024 resident population figures.

3.1.1 Importing the geospatial data

mpsz19 <- st_read("data/geospatial/MasterPlan2019SubzoneBoundaryNoSeaGEOJSON.geojson") %>%
  st_transform(crs = 3414)

Reading layer `URA_MP19_SUBZONE_NO_SEA_PL' from data source 
  `/Users/czxtom/Documents/Programming/GAA/ISSS626-GAA/Hands-on_Ex/Hands-on_Ex01/data/geospatial/MasterPlan2019SubzoneBoundaryNoSeaGEOJSON.geojson' 
  using driver `GeoJSON'
Simple feature collection with 332 features and 13 fields
Geometry type: MULTIPOLYGON
Dimension:     XY
Bounding box:  xmin: 103.6057 ymin: 1.158699 xmax: 104.0885 ymax: 1.470775
Geodetic CRS:  WGS 84




3.1.2 Checking the attributes

names(mpsz19)

 [1] "OBJECTID"   "SUBZONE_NO" "SUBZONE_N"  "SUBZONE_C"  "CA_IND"    
 [6] "PLN_AREA_N" "PLN_AREA_C" "REGION_N"   "REGION_C"   "INC_CRC"   
[11] "FMEL_UPD_D" "SHAPE.AREA" "SHAPE.LEN"  "geometry"  


The reference book at this point runs a chunk of rvest code to parse attributes out of an HTML table buried in a Description field. That was necessary for the KML version of this layer, which data.gov.sg has since unpublished. title: Hands-on Exercise 1
text:
3.2 Data Preparation
The target is one row per subzone with six fields. YOUNG is ages 0 to 24, ECONOMY ACTIVE is 25 to 64, and AGED is 65 and over. DEPENDENCY divides the young plus the aged by the economically active.
First the aggregate and pivot.

popdata2024 <- popdata %>%
  group_by(PA, SZ, AG) %>%
  summarise(`POP` = sum(`Pop`), .groups = "drop") %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = AG, values_from = POP)

Now a step the reference book does not take, and which turns out to matter a great deal.

names(popdata2024)

 [1] "PA"          "SZ"          "0_to_4"      "10_to_14"    "15_to_19"   
 [6] "20_to_24"    "25_to_29"    "30_to_34"    "35_to_39"    "40_to_44"   
[11] "45_to_49"    "50_to_54"    "55_to_59"    "5_to_9"      "60_to_64"   
[16] "65_to_69"    "70_to_74"    "75_to_79"    "80_to_84"    "85_to_89"   
[21] "90_and_over"


The book builds the three age bands by column number, like rowSums(.[3:6]) + rowSums(.[12]) for YOUNG. That only works if the age groups come out in a particular order. Look at the list above. They do not.
pivot_wider() names the new columns after the values it found, then those names get sorted as text. As text, 5_to_9 comes after 55_to_59, so it sits at position 14 instead of 12.
Run the book’s numbers against my columns and YOUNG grabs the 50 to 54 band instead of 5 to 9. ECONOMY ACTIVE ends up counting primary school children.






WarningIssue I hit



Like the projection one, this does not error. It just gives you a wrong dependency ratio, and every map after it looks completely normal.
I nearly skipped names(popdata2024). It was one line and it caught the whole thing.


Selecting by name instead removes the dependency on ordering entirely.

young_ag <- c("0_to_4", "5_to_9", "10_to_14", "15_to_19", "20_to_24")

active_ag <- c("25_to_29", "30_to_34", "35_to_39", "40_to_44",
               "45_to_49", "50_to_54", "55_to_59", "60_to_64")

aged_ag <- c("65_to_69", "70_to_74", "75_to_79",
             "80_to_84", "85_to_89", "90_and_over")

A guard against the same class of problem returning. If a future release renames or adds a band, this stops the render rather than letting a wrong number through.

stopifnot(all(c(young_ag, active_ag, aged_ag) %in% names(popdata2024)))


popdata2024 <- popdata2024 %>%
  mutate(
    YOUNG = rowSums(across(all_of(young_ag))),
    `ECONOMY ACTIVE` = rowSums(across(all_of(active_ag))),
    AGED = rowSums(across(all_of(aged_ag))),
    TOTAL = rowSums(across(all_of(c(young_ag, active_ag, aged_ag)))),
    DEPENDENCY = (YOUNG + AGED) / `ECONOMY ACTIVE`
  ) %>%
  select(`PA`, `SZ`, `YOUNG`, `ECONOMY ACTIVE`, `AGED`, `TOTAL`, `DEPENDENCY`)

Now a check. The three bands should add up to the total, and the ratio for Singapore overall should be somewhere near 0.7.

popdata2024 %>%
  summarise(
    young = sum(YOUNG),
    active = sum(`ECONOMY ACTIVE`),
    aged = sum(AGED),
    total = sum(TOTAL),
    bands_match_total = sum(YOUNG) + sum(`ECONOMY ACTIVE`) + sum(AGED) == sum(TOTAL),
    overall_dependency = (sum(YOUNG) + sum(AGED)) / sum(`ECONOMY ACTIVE`)
  )

# A tibble: 1 × 6
    young  active   aged   total bands_match_total overall_dependency
    <dbl>   <dbl>  <dbl>   <dbl> <lgl>                          <dbl>
1 1014400 2418550 756510 4189460 TRUE                           0.732








ImportantCheck that caught it



The bands add to 4,189,460 and Singapore’s published resident population is about 4.19 million, so that matches. The overall ratio is 0.732, which is in the right range.
Both had to be right before I trusted any map on this page. If I had used the book’s column numbers, this check is where it would have shown up.



3.2.1 Joining the attribute and geospatial data
The PA and SZ values are mixed case while PLN_AREA_N and SUBZONE_N are uppercase, so they will not match until we fix that.

popdata2024 <- popdata2024 %>%
  mutate_at(.vars = vars(PA, SZ), .funs = list(toupper)) %>%
  filter(`ECONOMY ACTIVE` > 0)


mpsz_pop2024 <- left_join(mpsz19, popdata2024,
                          by = c("SUBZONE_N" = "SZ"))

The sf object goes on the left of the join deliberately. That is what keeps the result an sf data frame rather than a plain tibble.

write_rds(mpsz_pop2024, "data/rds/mpsz_pop2024.rds")

3.3.1 The quick way, qtm()

The PlotThe Code

qtm(shp = mpsz_pop2024, fill = "DEPENDENCY",
    title = "The default bins, left exactly as qtm gives them")




qtm() is quick to write, but look at what the default bins did. The legend runs 0 to 10 in steps of two. Almost every subzone is under 1, so the whole island lands in the palest class and one dark polygon sits near Changi.
The map is not wrong. It just does not show anything.






NoteLearning diary



One subzone with a ratio of 10 is enough to wreck the default bins for all 332 of them. That is why the custom breaks section below matters.
It is also why I stopped using qtm() after this point. It is fine for a first look but it gives you no way to change the bins.




3.3.2 Drawing a base map

title: Hands-on Exercise 1
text:
3.4 Data Classification Methods
tmap offers ten classification styles. The choice matters more than it looks, because the same data can tell quite different stories depending on where the breaks fall.

3.4.1 Quantile

The PlotThe Code














tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "quantile", n = 5),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Dependency ratio")) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_title("Quantile puts an equal number of subzones in each class")






3.4.2 Equal interval

The PlotThe Code














tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "equal", n = 5),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Dependency ratio")) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_title("Equal interval hands almost every subzone to one class")




Same column, same data, two maps that look nothing alike.
Quantile puts the same number of subzones in each class, so the breaks come out at 0.64, 0.70, 0.74 and 0.82. Those all sit inside the range where the data actually is, and the map separates the central and eastern subzones clearly.
Equal interval cuts 0 to 10 into five equal parts. Nearly everything falls in the first one, so the island goes pale with a single dark polygon. If you only saw that map you would think dependency hardly varies in Singapore, which is not true.
Neither map is lying. They are the same numbers. But one subzone at 10 is enough to make the equal interval version useless, and I would not have known that without putting them side by side.


3.4.3 Custom breaks
Always look at the numbers before choosing break points.

summary(mpsz_pop2024$DEPENDENCY)

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max.     NAs 
 0.0000  0.6750  0.7283  0.7563  0.8140 10.0000      94 


Most values sit between 0.6 and 1.0, so breaks at 0.60, 0.70, 0.80 and 0.90 will separate the bulk of the data. Remember tmap needs n+1 values including a minimum and maximum.

The PlotThe Code














tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                breaks = c(0, 0.60, 0.70, 0.80, 0.90, 1.00)),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Dependency ratio")) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_title("Breaks chosen from the summary rather than by the default")

title: Hands-on Exercise 1
text:
3.7 Small Multiple Choropleth Maps
Facet maps put several maps side by side, which makes it easy to see how a spatial pattern shifts with another variable.

3.7.1 By passing multiple variables to an aesthetic

The PlotThe Code














tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = c("YOUNG", "AGED"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(position = tm_pos_in("right", "bottom")),
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "equal", n = 5,
                                              values = "brewer.blues")) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)






3.7.2 By arranging separate maps in a grid

The PlotThe Code














youngmap <- tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "YOUNG",
              fill.legend = tm_legend(position = tm_pos_in("right", "bottom")),
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "quantile",
                                              values = "brewer.blues")) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_title("Where the young live, as a raw count")

agedmap <- tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "AGED",
              fill.legend = tm_legend(position = tm_pos_in("right", "bottom")),
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "quantile",
                                              values = "brewer.blues")) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_title("Where the aged live, as a raw count")

tmap_arrange(youngmap, agedmap, asp = 1, ncol = 2)




The two maps look almost the same. I expected the aged map to light up the older estates and the young map to light up the newer towns, but the same subzones are dark on both.
That is because both are raw counts. A subzone with more people in it has more of everyone. So these maps are mostly showing where people live, not where the population is young or old.






TipAlternative explored



The book stops at the count maps. Since they were not answering my question, I redrew both as shares of each subzone’s own population instead.


Dividing each band by the subzone total takes population size out of it.

mpsz_pop2024 <- mpsz_pop2024 %>%
  mutate(`YOUNG PCT` = YOUNG / TOTAL * 100,
         `AGED PCT` = AGED / TOTAL * 100)


The PlotThe Code














youngpct <- tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "YOUNG PCT",
              fill.legend = tm_legend(position = tm_pos_in("right", "bottom")),
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "quantile",
                                              values = "brewer.blues")) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_title("Young as a share of the subzone")

agedpct <- tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "AGED PCT",
              fill.legend = tm_legend(position = tm_pos_in("right", "bottom")),
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "quantile",
                                              values = "brewer.blues")) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_title("Aged as a share of the subzone")

tmap_arrange(youngpct, agedpct, asp = 1, ncol = 2)




Now the two maps look different, which is what I expected the first pair to show. Read them against the count maps above to see how much of that first pattern was just population size.


3.7.3 By a group-by variable in tm_facets()

The PlotThe Code














tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_fill(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
          fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "quantile",
                                          values = "brewer.blues"),
          fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Dependency ratio")) +
  tm_facets(by = "REGION_N", nrow = 2, ncols = 3,
            free.coords = TRUE, drop.units = TRUE) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_title("Dependency by region, each panel on its own extent")

3.9 Complementing the Map with a Statistical Chart
A map shows where, a chart shows how much. fill.chart puts both in one figure.

The PlotThe Code














mpsz_pop2024 %>%
  filter(REGION_N == "CENTRAL REGION") %>%
  tm_shape() +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "quantile",

  tm_layout(asp = 0.8)




The boxplot shows something the map does not. All the outliers are below the box, near zero, not above it. Those are subzones with working age residents and hardly any children or elderly.
Once labelled, they turn out to be bunched in the downtown core. The labels overlap a lot at this size and would need fixing before I used this anywhere, but you can still see where they are.

  filter(REGION_N == "CENTRAL REGION")

stats <- boxplot.stats(mpsz_selected_central$DEPENDENCY)

  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",

3.10 Creating an Interactive Map
Switching tmap_mode() to view turns the same code into a zoomable, clickable map.

The PlotThe Code












region_selected <- mpsz_pop2024 %>%
  filter(REGION_N == "CENTRAL REGION")
region_bbox <- st_bbox(region_selected)

stats <- boxplot.stats(region_selected$DEPENDENCY)
outlier_vals <- stats$out
outlier_sf <- region_selected[region_selected$DEPENDENCY %in% outlier_vals, ]

tmap_mode("view")
tm_shape(region_selected, bbox = region_bbox) +
  tm_fill("DEPENDENCY",
          id = "SUBZONE_N",
          popup.vars = c("Name" = "SUBZONE_N",
                         "Dependency" = "DEPENDENCY")) +
  tm_borders() +
  tm_shape(outlier_sf) +
  tm_borders(col = "red", lwd = 2) +
  tm_view(set_zoom_limits = c(12, 14))




set_zoom_limits is doing real work here. Total freedom to zoom sounds generous but in practice users end up lost somewhere over the ocean, so bounding the range keeps them inside the study area.

tmap_mode("plot")

title: Hands-on Exercise 1
text:
4.1 Is this actually spatial analysis?
Anselin’s lecture gives a test for this. If you move things around and nothing changes, it was not spatial analysis. If it does change, it was.
Easy enough to run on my own data. sample() only reshuffles which subzone holds which number, so every value is preserved.

set.seed(1234)
mpsz_shuffled <- mpsz_pop2024
mpsz_shuffled$DEPENDENCY <- sample(mpsz_pop2024$DEPENDENCY)

If the values are the same, any summary that ignores location should be identical.

tibble(
  version  = c("Real Singapore", "Same numbers, shuffled"),
  subzones = c(sum(!is.na(mpsz_pop2024$DEPENDENCY)),
               sum(!is.na(mpsz_shuffled$DEPENDENCY))),
  mean     = c(mean(mpsz_pop2024$DEPENDENCY, na.rm = TRUE),
               mean(mpsz_shuffled$DEPENDENCY, na.rm = TRUE)),
  sd       = c(sd(mpsz_pop2024$DEPENDENCY, na.rm = TRUE),
               sd(mpsz_shuffled$DEPENDENCY, na.rm = TRUE)),
  median   = c(median(mpsz_pop2024$DEPENDENCY, na.rm = TRUE),
               median(mpsz_shuffled$DEPENDENCY, na.rm = TRUE))
) %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~round(.x, 4)))

# A tibble: 2 × 5
  version                subzones  mean    sd median
  <chr>                     <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl>
1 Real Singapore              238 0.756 0.625  0.728
2 Same numbers, shuffled      238 0.756 0.625  0.728


Same for the histogram.

The PlotThe Code














bind_rows(
  tibble(version = "Real Singapore",         value = mpsz_pop2024$DEPENDENCY),
  tibble(version = "Same numbers, shuffled", value = mpsz_shuffled$DEPENDENCY)
) %>%
  filter(!is.na(value), value < 2) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = value)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "#0072B2", colour = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  facet_wrap(~version) +
  labs(title = "The same histogram twice",
       subtitle = "Values under 2 only, so the single subzone at 10 does not flatten the axis",
       x = "Dependency ratio", y = "Subzones") +
  theme_minimal()




Now the maps.

The PlotThe Code














shuffle_map <- function(dat, ttl) {
  tm_shape(dat) +
    tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
                fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "quantile", n = 5,
                                                values = "brewer.blues"),
                fill.legend = tm_legend(show = FALSE)) +
    tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.4) +
    tm_title(ttl, size = 0.9)
}

tmap_arrange(shuffle_map(mpsz_pop2024,  "Real Singapore"),
             shuffle_map(mpsz_shuffled, "Same numbers, shuffled"),
             ncol = 2)










NoteLearning diary



Every number is the same. The mean, the spread, the median, the histogram. And the two maps look nothing alike.
So whatever the difference is between those two pictures, none of the statistics I know how to compute can see it. That gap is what the rest of this course is for. Lesson 4 defines what neighbouring means and Lesson 5 turns this difference into a single number I can test.
It also answers something I had wondered at the start, which was why not just do this in pandas. A non-spatial toolkit would tell me these two datasets are identical, because on everything it can measure, they are.

text:
4.2 Does the pattern survive a change of unit?
This is the Modifiable Areal Unit Problem. Results shift when you change the size or the shape of the units you are measuring on.
Singapore’s subzones sit inside planning areas, so I can test the size half of it directly.

mpsz_pa <- mpsz_pop2024 %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  filter(!is.na(TOTAL)) %>%
  group_by(PLN_AREA_N) %>%
  summarise(YOUNG  = sum(YOUNG),
            ACTIVE = sum(`ECONOMY ACTIVE`),
            AGED   = sum(AGED),
            n_subzones = n(),
            .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(DEPENDENCY_PA = (YOUNG + AGED) / ACTIVE) %>%
  filter(is.finite(DEPENDENCY_PA))


tibble(
  unit   = c("Subzone", "Planning area"),
  n      = c(sum(!is.na(mpsz_pop2024$DEPENDENCY)), nrow(mpsz_pa)),
  min    = c(min(mpsz_pop2024$DEPENDENCY, na.rm = TRUE),    min(mpsz_pa$DEPENDENCY_PA)),
  median = c(median(mpsz_pop2024$DEPENDENCY, na.rm = TRUE), median(mpsz_pa$DEPENDENCY_PA)),
  max    = c(max(mpsz_pop2024$DEPENDENCY, na.rm = TRUE),    max(mpsz_pa$DEPENDENCY_PA))
) %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~round(.x, 3)))

The planning area curve is taller and narrower. Same people, same formula, and the extremes have gone.
A map drawn at planning area level would make Singapore look far more even than it is. Neither unit is the right one. All I can do is say which one I used and admit the answer depends on it.
I could only test the size half of MAUP. The other half is that results also change when you redraw the boundaries at the same size, and I have no alternative zoning to try that with.

text:
4.3 Who does the map actually show?
A choropleth colours areas, and the eye reads area as amount. So a big empty subzone shouts while a small crowded one whispers.
That is measurable.

mpsz_pop2024 %>%
  filter(!is.na(TOTAL)) %>%
  mutate(area_km2 = as.numeric(st_area(.)) / 1e6) %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  summarise(
    `Map area held by the least populated half of subzones (%)` =
      round(sum(area_km2[TOTAL <= median(TOTAL)]) / sum(area_km2) * 100, 1),
    `Population those same subzones hold (%)` =
      round(sum(TOTAL[TOTAL <= median(TOTAL)]) / sum(TOTAL) * 100, 1)
  ) %>%
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "measure", values_to = "value")

# A tibble: 2 × 2
  measure                                                   value
  <chr>                                                     <dbl>
1 Map area held by the least populated half of subzones (%)  53.4
2 Population those same subzones hold (%)                    12.5








NoteLearning diary



Put those two numbers next to each other and the map stops looking neutral. Anyone reading it is weighting land, not people.
This is the same problem as the young and aged count maps further up, arriving from a different direction. There I was mapping counts when I wanted rates. Here I am mapping rates but the canvas itself is weighted by area.

title: Hands-on Exercise 1
text:
4.4 Limitations
Worth stating what this does not cover.

Part 1 uses the 2014 Master Plan boundaries and Part 2 uses 2019, because that is what the chapters specify. Subzone definitions changed between them, so the pre-school counts and the dependency ratios are not measured on quite the same geography.
94 subzones have no population data and are grey on every map. They are dropped rather than shown as zero.
The dependency ratio treats 25 to 64 as working age. That is a convention, not a fact, and it is drifting.
Point in polygon counting ignores catchments. A pre-school just over a subzone boundary serves those children anyway.
Only the scale half of MAUP is tested, as noted above.







WarningIssue I hit



na.rm = TRUE does not remove Inf. I assumed it did.
If a subzone has residents but nobody of working age, the dependency ratio divides by zero and gives Inf, and then mean(x, na.rm = TRUE) returns Inf for the whole column. is.finite() is the filter that actually catches it.
My data avoids this because I filtered on ECONOMY ACTIVE > 0 before the join, but that was luck rather than intent.

1.1 Installing and Loading R Packages

title: Hands-on Exercise 2
text:
2.3 Clark-Evans Test
The Clark-Evans index R compares the average nearest neighbour distance to what it would be under complete spatial randomness. Below 1 means clustered, above 1 means spread out, around 1 means random.

H0: childcare centres are randomly distributed.
H1: childcare centres are not randomly distributed.


clarkevans.test(childcareSG_ppp,
                correction = "none",
                alternative = "clustered")


    Clark-Evans test
    No edge correction
    Z-test

data:  childcareSG_ppp
R = 0.53532, p-value < 2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: clustered (R < 1)


Now the same test with the p-value from simulation rather than from a normal approximation.

clarkevans.test(childcareSG_ppp,
                correction = "none",
                alternative = "clustered",
                method = "MonteCarlo",
                nsim = 99)


    Clark-Evans test
    No edge correction
    Monte Carlo test based on 99 simulations of CSR with fixed n

data:  childcareSG_ppp
R = 0.53532, p-value = 0.01
alternative hypothesis: clustered (R < 1)








ImportantCheck that caught it



The two p-values are not the same and they cannot be. The Monte Carlo version compares R against 99 simulated patterns, so the smallest p-value it can possibly report is 0.01. It is not more or less significant than the first, it is a different test with a floor set by how many simulations I asked for.
The required reading gives the rule. For a two-sided test, alpha works out as 2 divided by the number of simulations plus 1, so 39 simulations gives 5 percent. Every simulation count in this exercise is therefore a choice about alpha, and the book changes it between sections without comment.








CautionWhere I disagree with the exercise



R comes out well below 1 and the p-value is tiny, so the test says clustered. I am not sure that tells me much.
The null here is that childcare centres could be anywhere in Singapore with equal probability. That includes reservoirs, the airport, industrial land and military areas. Childcare centres go where children live.
Floch et al. make exactly this point about pharmacies in France, whose locations are regulated by population, and conclude the CSR reference “does not appear to be the most relevant in this case”. I think the same applies here. I come back to it in Part 3 with a null that is not a strawman.

text:
3.1 G Function
G measures the distance from each point to its nearest neighbour, then plots the cumulative distribution of those distances. A curve above the theoretical line means neighbours are closer than random, so clustered.

The PlotThe Code














G_CK <- Gest(childcare_ck_ppp, correction = "border")
plot(G_CK, xlim = c(0, 500),
     main = "G function, Choa Chu Kang")





H0: childcare centres in Choa Chu Kang are randomly distributed.
H1: they are not.

Reject if p is below 0.001.

The PlotThe Code














G_CK.csr <- envelope(childcare_ck_ppp, Gest, nsim = 999, verbose = FALSE)
plot(G_CK.csr, main = "G against 999 simulations of CSR, Choa Chu Kang")










CautionWhere I disagree with the exercise



The grey band is not a confidence interval, even though it is drawn like one and everyone reads it as one.
Floch et al. are explicit. “The envelope should not be interpreted as a confidence interval around the indicator being studied: it indicates the critical values of the test.” It is the range the simulated patterns covered, not a range of plausible values for my curve.
I have written the captions to say critical values rather than confidence, because the difference changes what the picture is claiming.



The PlotThe Code














G_tm <- Gest(childcare_tm_ppp, correction = "best")
plot(G_tm, main = "G function, Tampines")

title: Hands-on Exercise 2
text:
3.2 F Function
F is the mirror image. Instead of measuring from each point to its nearest neighbour, it drops a grid of arbitrary locations and measures from each of those to the nearest point. It maps empty space rather than occupied space.

The PlotThe Code














F_CK <- Fest(childcare_ck_ppp)
plot(F_CK, main = "F function, Choa Chu Kang")





The PlotThe Code














F_CK.csr <- envelope(childcare_ck_ppp, Fest, nsim = 999, verbose = FALSE)
plot(F_CK.csr, main = "F against 999 simulations of CSR, Choa Chu Kang")










NoteLearning diary



G and F point opposite ways for the same pattern, which confused me until I drew it out.
Clustered points have close neighbours, so G climbs fast. But clustering also leaves big empty gaps, so a random location is far from any point and F climbs slowly. Clustered means G above the line and F below it. Once I had that straight the two plots stopped looking contradictory.



The PlotThe Code














F_tm <- Fest(childcare_tm_ppp, correction = "best")
plot(F_tm, main = "F function, Tampines")

title: Hands-on Exercise 2
text:
3.3 K Function
G and F only look at the nearest neighbour. K counts every neighbour within distance r, for every r, so it works at all scales at once.

The PlotThe Code














K_ck <- Kest(childcare_ck_ppp, correction = "Ripley")
plot(K_ck, . - r ~ r,
     ylab = "K(d) - r", xlab = "d (m)",
     main = "K function, Choa Chu Kang")





The PlotThe Code














K_ck.csr <- envelope(childcare_ck_ppp, Kest, nsim = 99, rank = 1,
                     glocal = TRUE, verbose = FALSE)
plot(K_ck.csr, . - r ~ r, xlab = "d", ylab = "K(d) - r",
     main = "K against CSR, global envelope, Choa Chu Kang")










WarningIssue I hit



glocal = TRUE appears here and for L, but not for G or F earlier. I copied it across without noticing, then went back to work out what it does.
The test is repeated at every value of r. Running the same test at dozens of values of r, then reporting the ones that cross, inflates the false positive rate well above the stated alpha. A global envelope corrects for that. A pointwise one does not.
So the G and F results above are on a weaker footing than the K and L results below, and the book never says so. I redo one of them properly in Part 3.



The PlotThe Code














K_tm <- Kest(childcare_tm_ppp, correction = "Ripley")
plot(K_tm, . - r ~ r, ylab = "K(d) - r", xlab = "d (m)",
     xlim = c(0, 1000), main = "K function, Tampines")

title: Hands-on Exercise 2
text:
3.4 L Function
L is K with the shape taken out. K under randomness grows as pi r squared, which is a curve and hard to eyeball. L is the square root of K over pi, so under randomness it is a straight line, and plotting L(r) - r makes randomness a flat line at zero.

The PlotThe Code














L_ck <- Lest(childcare_ck_ppp, correction = "Ripley")
plot(L_ck, . - r ~ r, ylab = "L(d) - r", xlab = "d (m)",
     main = "L function, Choa Chu Kang")










NoteLearning diary



Floch et al. give the reading of L(r) - r that finally made it concrete for me. If the curve reaches 2 at a radius of 1, there are as many neighbours within 1 unit of each point as a random pattern would put within 3 units.
So the height of the curve is not an abstract test statistic. It is how much further you would have to walk, under randomness, to meet the same number of neighbours.



The PlotThe Code














L_ck.csr <- envelope(childcare_ck_ppp, Lest, nsim = 99, rank = 1,
                     glocal = TRUE, verbose = FALSE)
plot(L_ck.csr, . - r ~ r, xlab = "d", ylab = "L(d) - r",
     main = "L against CSR, global envelope, Choa Chu Kang")





The PlotThe Code














L_tm <- Lest(childcare_tm_ppp, correction = "Ripley")
plot(L_tm, . - r ~ r, ylab = "L(d) - r", xlab = "d (m)",
     xlim = c(0, 1000), main = "L function, Tampines")

title: Hands-on Exercise 2
section: 4.1 Testing Against a Null That Is Not a Strawman
text:
4.1 Testing Against a Null That Is Not a Strawman
Everything so far compares childcare centres to a pattern where any point in Singapore is equally likely. Reservoirs, the airport, Jurong Island, military land.
Floch et al. raise this about pharmacies in France, whose siting is set by regulation tied to population, and say plainly that CSR “does not appear to be the most relevant” reference there. Childcare centres are the same kind of thing. They follow housing.
So the finding that they are clustered may be telling me only that Singapore’s residents are clustered, which I already knew.
The reading offers a fix. Kinhom() drops the assumption that intensity is constant and compares the pattern against a null with the intensity actually observed. If the centres still clump beyond that, the clustering is real. If they stop, it was population all along.

lambda_ck <- density(childcare_ck_ppp, sigma = bw.diggle, edge = TRUE)
range(lambda_ck$v, na.rm = TRUE)

[1] 5.030384e-10 4.086766e-05








NoteLearning diary



My surface comes out entirely positive, so nothing here needs fixing. I am clamping anyway, and the reason is worth writing down.
Look at the book’s own output in section 4.7.1. Its density range starts at -6.58e-21. That is floating point noise from the edge correction rather than a real negative density, and it is invisible when you plot the surface.
It stops mattering right up until you feed the surface to rpoispp() for the simulation below, which refuses a negative intensity with a “negative probability” error that says nothing about where the negative came from. Whether you hit it depends on your data.
One line now is cheaper than working that out later.



lambda_pos <- lambda_ck
lambda_pos$v[lambda_pos$v < 0] <- 0

# confirm whether the clamp actually had anything to do
sum(lambda_ck$v < 0, na.rm = TRUE)

[1] 0



The PlotThe Code














Kinhom_ck <- Kinhom(childcare_ck_ppp, lambda = lambda_pos,
                    correction = "Ripley")
plot(Kinhom_ck, . - r ~ r, ylab = "Kinhom(d) - r", xlab = "d (m)",
     main = "Inhomogeneous K, intensity taken from the data")





The PlotThe Code














Kinhom_ck.csr <- envelope(childcare_ck_ppp, Kinhom,
                          simulate = expression(rpoispp(lambda_pos)),
                          nsim = 39, verbose = FALSE)
plot(Kinhom_ck.csr, . - r ~ r, xlab = "d", ylab = "Kinhom(d) - r",
     main = "Inhomogeneous K against a population-shaped null")










TipAlternative explored



This is the same K function against a different question. Kest asks whether centres are more clustered than a uniform scatter. Kinhom asks whether they are more clustered than the local intensity already implies.
Compare this plot against the Kest one further up. Whatever gap remains here is clustering that population density does not explain, and that is the interesting part.
The caveat is that the null is estimated from the same data it is tested against, so it is not independent evidence. Floch et al. flag exactly this, warning that bias appears when the smoothing window is close in size to the r values being tested.

title: Hands-on Exercise 2
text:
4.2 Cumulative Against Density
K counts every neighbour out to r. That is cumulative, so a bump at 400 metres could be caused by tight clustering at 50 metres that is still being carried along in the total.
The pair correlation function is the same idea measured in a ring at distance r rather than a disc out to r, so it shows where clustering actually happens rather than where it has accumulated.

The PlotThe Code














pcf_ck <- pcf(childcare_ck_ppp)
plot(pcf_ck, main = "Pair correlation, Choa Chu Kang",
     xlab = "d (m)")
abline(h = 1, lty = 2, col = "#D55E00")










TipAlternative explored



Under randomness the pair correlation sits at 1, which is the dashed line. Above 1 means more neighbours at that exact distance than chance would give.
The advantage over K is that it localises. The disadvantage is that a cumulative function can spot clusters of clusters and a density function cannot. They answer different questions and neither replaces the other.

title: Hands-on Exercise 2
section: 4.3 Redoing G With a Global Envelope
text:
4.3 Redoing G With a Global Envelope
The G test in Part 2 used a pointwise envelope, which inflates the false positive rate across all the r values tested. Same test, corrected.

The PlotThe Code














G_ck.global <- envelope(childcare_ck_ppp, Gest, nsim = 39, rank = 1,
                        global = TRUE, verbose = FALSE)
plot(G_ck.global, main = "G with a global envelope, Choa Chu Kang")










TipAlternative explored



The global band is wider than the pointwise one, which is the correction doing its job. It is harder to reject the null, and that is the point.
If the curve still leaves the band, the result survives the multiple testing problem. If it no longer does, the original finding was partly an artefact of testing at every r and reporting the crossings.

title: Hands-on Exercise 2
text:
4.4 A Second Opinion on Randomness
Everything so far is distance based. A quadrat test is the other family, dividing the region into cells and comparing counts against a Poisson expectation.

quadrat_ck <- quadrat.test(childcare_ck_ppp, nx = 4, ny = 4)
quadrat_ck


    Chi-squared test of CSR using quadrat counts

data:  childcare_ck_ppp
X2 = 21.603, df = 12, p-value = 0.08444
alternative hypothesis: two.sided

Quadrats: 13 tiles (irregular windows)








WarningIssue I hit



I first stored this as qt, which is base R’s t-distribution quantile function. R refused with “cannot change value of locked binding”.
Same class of mistake as naming something c or df. Worth checking a name is free before using it.








ImportantCheck that caught it



The quadrat test does not agree with Clark-Evans, and that is the most useful result in Part 3.
Clark-Evans gave R of 0.84 with p of 0.0089, so it rejected randomness for Choa Chu Kang. The quadrat test on the same points gives p of 0.084, so it does not. Two tests, one dataset, opposite conclusions at the five percent level.
Neither is wrong. They measure different things. Clark-Evans looks at nearest neighbour distances, so it notices points sitting in tight pairs. The quadrat test only counts how many points fall in each cell, so a pattern can be clumpy inside cells and still spread evenly across them.
Note the tile count too. I asked for a four by four grid, so sixteen cells, and the output says thirteen tiles and twelve degrees of freedom. Three cells fell outside the planning area boundary and were dropped, and twelve is thirteen minus one. So the grid I specified is not the grid that was tested.








TipAlternative explored



The quadrat answer depends entirely on the grid I picked, and a different nx and ny would move it.
That is the Modifiable Areal Unit Problem again, the same thing I hit in Exercise 1 aggregating subzones up to planning areas. Avoiding it is one of the main reasons the reading gives for preferring distance-based methods.

title: Hands-on Exercise 2
text:
4.5 Limitations

Every test in Parts 1 and 2 uses CSR as the null, which for a facility that follows housing is a weak comparison. Part 3 addresses this for one planning area only, not the whole island.
The Kinhom null is estimated from the same data it tests. It is a better question than CSR, not an independent one.
Simulation counts vary through the exercise, 99 here and 999 there, and each choice sets a different alpha.
The four planning areas come from the book. They are not a sample of anything, so nothing here generalises to Singapore’s other planning areas.
First and second order effects cannot be separated from a single observed pattern. That one is not fixable here and it undercuts the whole document, which is why it is also the second point in the reflections.
